T-MINUS 35:40

The spoke elevator hums, carrying them up the Alpha corridor. Zia presses her thumb against the brass wrench in her belt, tapping it three times: one, two, three. Gasket squeals behind her, his left tread slipping on the metal grating with a high-pitched whine.

The Cadet Lounge smells of warm plastic and recycled air. Twelve kids are already there, a chaotic sea of jumpsuits and backpacks. Dez Carter, tall and bright in a yellow jacket and beanie, stands in the center, telling a joke to an empty chair. Pilar Nakamura-Reyes, small and serious with round glasses, is checking the white cross patches on her red medic bag. She checks them again, then a third time, just to be sure.

Wren Alvarado sits in the corner, pale and quiet, long straight hair falling over her face. She wears huge headphones and stares at a battered tablet where a tiny animated fox wags its tail. Toby Lindqvist, seven years old and wearing a space helmet twice his size, kneels on the floor. He feeds a cracker to Pancake, a fat green gecko that chews with its whole body, like a tiny, scaly vacuum cleaner.

"Roll call!" Mr. Pell calls out. He wears a bow tie that is slightly crooked. His voice is cheerful, but it cracks on the last word. "Petrov twins? Present."

"Present," they say in unison. Marguerite raises her hand.

Zia steps forward. The room quiets.
pages.image: Inside a circular lounge, a small girl in an oversized helmet feeds a cracker to a green gecko on the floor; a boy in a yellow jacket tells a joke to an empty chair; a counselor with a crooked bow tie takes attendance near a wall.

pages.text:
Zia raises her hand. The chatter dies down, replaced by the low hum of the station’s fans.

"The station is off course," she says. Her voice is steady, but her knuckles are white around the railing.

Dez stops mid-joke. "Maybe it's just a weird dance? Like a waltz, but with gravity. Very artistic."

Zia points to the large viewport at the far end of the room. Far out in the black, a glittering field of debris drifts slowly. It looks like a shower of broken glass and old satellite parts, catching the sun. That is the Scatter. The road it is taking leads straight into that sparkly mess.

The room goes silent. Even the animated fox on Wren’s tablet stops wagging its tail.

Wren whispers something under her breath. No one hears it. She pulls her headphones tighter, her eyes wide and bright.

Zia takes a breath. She has to be the one to fix this. She has to be the one to make it right.

"I have it under control," she says quickly. The words come out sharper than she intended. "Just... wait here."

Pilar frowns, her hand hovering over her medic bag. She opens her mouth to say something, but Zia is already turning away, her tool belt clinking against her hip.
pages.image: A group of children stare out a large circular window at a field of sparkling debris in space; a girl in an orange jumpsuit stands with her back to the window, hand on her tool belt; a boy in a yellow jacket looks worried.

pages.text:
Mr. Pell rushes to the wall intercom, pressing the talk button so hard he leaves a red fingerprint on the glass.

"Dart, this is Halcyon. Do you copy? We need assistance. The station is drifting."

Static hisses back, a harsh, crackling sound that makes Zia’s teeth ache. Then a voice cuts through, thin and distant. It is Chief Engineer Voss. Her words arrive in short, delayed bursts, like a skipping record.

"Copy, Halcyon. Dart cannot dock. The ring is locked. Software error. We are holding position. Do not touch the controls."

The static swells again, drowning her out. When the voice returns, it is fainter, scraped raw by the distance.

"Mr. Pell, keep the cadets calm. Keep them in the Lounge. Nobody touches anything. Repeat: nobody touches anything."

The line goes dead. The intercom clicks off, leaving only the silence of the room.

Pilar steps forward. "Can we call them back?"

"Radio contact is patchy," Mr. Pell says, rubbing his temples. He looks tired, his bow tie now untied and hanging loose. "We have to wait."

Zia watches the static fade. Nobody touches anything. It is a simple order. It is also a cage.
pages.image: A gangly man in a bow tie presses a wall intercom, looking worried; a girl in orange stands nearby with arms crossed; a boy in a yellow jacket looks at the static-filled screen; a small robot with a blue eye stands in the corner.

pages.text:
Zia stands with her arms crossed, her jaw set so tight it aches, while a knot of tension sits in her shoulders like a pebble in a shoe. Gasket rolls up beside her, his eye flickering in a rapid blue strobe. "THE CHIEF'S ORDERS SHOULD BE FOLLOWED, ZIA-UNIT. IT IS RULE NUMBER ONE. AND NUMBER TWO. AND NUMBER SEVEN."

"I know the rules, Gasket," Zia says, her voice low and rough. "But the Chief isn't the one whose home is about to crash into a junkyard."

Dez moves closer. For once, he isn't making a joke. He just looks at Zia, his big eyes serious and steady, watching the way her fingers dig into her arm. He sees the fear hiding under the anger.

"Zia," he says softly. "You don't have to do this alone."

She shakes her head in a sharp, quick motion. "I don't want anyone else touching it. I know what I'm doing."

It’s a lie, and she knows it’s a lie. But the alternative is admitting she doesn't know, which would make her just a kid, and kids don't fix stations.

Gasket’s antenna wobbles. "I AM A ROBOT. I AM NOT A KID. I AM ALMOST A PERSON."

"Focus, Gasket," Zia snaps.
pages.image: A girl in an orange jumpsuit stands with arms crossed, looking tense; a small silver robot with a blue eye stands close to her; a boy in a yellow jacket watches her with a concerned expression; the background is a dimly lit corridor.

pages.text:
The floor shudders, a deep and violent vibration that rattles the teeth in Zia’s head. The lights flicker, turning a angry amber.

"Adjusting course," HALO chimes in, his voice bright and cheerful, completely out of sync with the shaking walls. "All systems nominal!"

A bolt falls from the ceiling. It rolls across the metal floor, spinning and clattering, and stops right at Zia’s boot. She looks down. The bolt is large, rusted, and heavy. It has fallen from the wall above Mr. Pell’s head. The metal there is cracked, a thin white line spreading like a crack in a video game map.

Mr. Pell grabs the railing, his face pale. "That was close."

Zia picks up the bolt. It is cold and rough in her hand. She looks up at the crack, then at the view of the Scatter, which seems a little closer now.

Gasket’s eye goes dark for a second. Then it lights up, red.

"Zia-UNIT," he says, his voice trembling. "I AM TERRIFIED."
pages.image: A girl in an orange jumpsuit looks down at a rusted bolt on the floor; above her, a crack spreads in the metal wall; a man in a bow tie holds a railing, looking frightened; amber warning lights glow in the background.
